core_principles.text: Proper lunge depth occurs when the back knee gently touches or comes very close to the ground under control.
Standardize the range of motion across all repetitions from the start to the end of a set to reliably track progress.
Step long enough to feel a stretch in the glutes, adductors, and quads while keeping the front foot stable.
Lunge only as far as allows secure footing and balance so force production is not compromised.
Take about 2 seconds to descend all the way down in control to expose muscles to eccentric stress and stabilize both legs.
Keep the upper body upright and still, especially toward the bottom of the lunge, by bracing the core.
Resetting by bringing the feet together after every lunge helps regain balance and allows carrying heavier loads with good technique.
Use straps, grips, chalk, or switch to a barbell lunge if hand grip strength becomes the limiting factor instead of the target leg muscles.
Choose a weight that permits performing more than around 10 but less than around 35 lunges in one set without taking breaks.

common_mistakes.text: Cutting depth by failing to perform a full range of motion and not going all the way down.
Failing to standardize range of motion across reps, making progress tracking inaccurate.
Taking too short of a step during walking lunges.
Descending in an uncontrolled manner during the eccentric portion of the lunge.
Tilting the upper body forward at the bottom of the lunge.

specific_findings.text: Take about 2 seconds to descend all the way down in control during the lunge.
Choose a weight that allows performing more than around 10 but less than around 35 lunges in one set without taking breaks for optimal hypertrophy stimulus.

consequences.text: Cutting depth reduces muscle growth and motor unit recruitment because muscles grow more when stretched through a full range of motion.
Taking steps that are too short can cause discomfort in the knee and fails to recruit all target muscles.
Taking steps that are too long causes instability and reduces the amount of force you can produce.
An uncontrolled descent can damage the knees, increase injury risk under heavy loads, and reduce muscle growth by bypassing eccentric tension.
Tilting forward shifts the workload off the intended target musculature and onto the back and hamstrings.

core_principles.text: Adjust technique and loading so that the target muscles, including the glutes, hamstrings, and adductors, are properly engaged and serve as the limiting factor during lunges.

common_mistakes.text: Failing to feel or work the target muscles, such as the glutes, hamstrings, and adductors, during the exercise.
